title: OpenAI promotes fair-use arguments in its New York Times dispute
dek: OpenAI published supporting briefs on AI training; a neutral court record sets out the publishers' objections over copied work and lost readership.

sources.title: Opinion, April 4, 2025, The New York Times Co. v. Microsoft et al., 23-cv-11195 (SHS), pp. 5, 7–9 and 20–24
sources.publisher: U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York

lede: OpenAI published excerpts from supporting fair-use briefs on October 30 in its dispute involving The New York Times. The arguments concern whether training on copyrighted material requires permission, a question that affects developers' data sourcing and publishers' licensing businesses.

facts.label: Parties
facts.value: OpenAI and The New York Times

body.text: OpenAI's selection includes Authors Alliance, Public Knowledge and the United States government. The company argues that fair use supports AI training. The court's April 2025 opinion records the publishers' opposing account: their works were used in training and reproduced in outputs, potentially substituting for visits to their websites. That puts subscription, advertising and licensing revenue at the center of the disagreement.

Training and generated answers present different questions for a software team. A decision about one use would need to be read for its scope before being applied to another. Developers should keep separate records of training inputs, retrieved material and displayed output, so a change in one area does not leave the whole product's data history tangled together.

claims.text: The October 30 publication presents arguments, not a new ruling or settlement.
The publishers' copying and market-harm allegations are recorded in a procedural opinion; that document does not establish them as proven infringement.
